title: Time-Sensitive Medicines Protocol
summary: How we identify time-sensitive medicines with the prescriber or pharmacist, write a plan for each one, plan, allocate and protect the visits that give them, monitor those visits in real time, and act when a dose is at risk of being late or missed. For care staff, Care Coordinators, staff who allocate visits, and managers.

keyPoints.intro: Some medicines, such as Parkinson's medicines, insulin and epilepsy medicines, can cause serious harm within hours if a dose is late or missed. These are the rules for every visit where one is due.
points: A time-sensitive medicine is flagged on the eMAR with its time and window. Give it first, within the window, and record it straight away so the actual time is shown.

If you may be late for a time-critical visit, phone the office (On-call Manager out of hours) as soon as you know, once parked with the engine off, not when you arrive. The office decides whether someone else goes.
If the window has closed, or will close before you can give the dose, phone the office before giving it and follow the advice. Never give a late or double dose on your own judgement.
If you arrive before the window opens, do other tasks first and give the dose when it opens. If your visit would end before then, phone the office.
Never swap, move or shorten a time-critical visit, or agree a new time with the person or family. Ask the office, which checks the window first.
If the dose is declined, the person is asleep and not to be woken, cannot swallow, or the medicine is missing, record it and phone the office before you leave, saying first that it is time-sensitive.
If nobody answers at a time-critical visit, phone the office within 5 minutes of arriving and follow the No Reply, No Access and Missing Person Procedure. Never leave until the office says you may.
Call 999 for the danger signs in the person's plan, such as low blood sugar not improving after a second treatment, or a person who is hard to wake, then tell the office.
On a double-handed visit, give the time-sensitive dose yourself if you are signed off for it; do not wait for your colleague.
A time-sensitive dose given outside its window, or missed, at your visit is a medicines incident: enter it in the incident log before your shift ends.
Tell the office the same day when a time-sensitive medicine has 7 days' supply or less and no new supply is in the home.

blocks.p: Some medicines must be given at a set time because a late or missed dose can cause serious harm within hours. NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service guidance notes that for a person with Parkinson's disease a delay of as little as 30 minutes can be the difference between functioning well and being unable to move, walk, talk or swallow. Late or missed insulin or epilepsy medicines can also cause serious harm. In home care, a late or missed visit means a late or missed dose. {{organisation}} identifies every time-sensitive medicine we support, protects the visits that give them and acts at once when a dose is at risk.

The law requires the proper and safe management of medicines (Regulation 12(2)(g) of the Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014). Guidance based on NICE guideline NG67 expects directions for a time-sensitive medicine to state what it is for, the dose and the time agreed with the person, and expects home care providers to let care workers prioritise visits to people who need these medicines. This protocol adds the detail to the Medicines Management Policy and applies its default window and 15-minute escalation rule.

bullets: Every time-sensitive medicine we support is confirmed with the prescriber or pharmacist, flagged, and has a written plan for late or missed doses.
Time-critical visits are planned, allocated and changed so each dose falls within its window.
A late care worker is noticed within 15 minutes and someone competent is sent; every late or missed dose gets clinical advice, is reported and is learned from.

blocks.p: This protocol applies to every employee, including bank and agency workers placed with us, who assesses, plans, allocates, monitors or carries out visits at which a time-sensitive medicine is supported, and to the managers who audit them. It covers time-sensitive medicines we support at Level 1, 2 or 3, and Level 0 medicines whose timing depends on our visit, such as insulin a person injects before a meal we prepare.

Care workers give insulin and other injections only as Level 3 tasks under the Delegated Healthcare Activities and Specialised Medicines Tasks Policy; this protocol sets their timing. Declined doses follow the Consent, Mental Capacity and Declined Medicines Policy, and recording follows the Medicines Administration Records (MAR and eMAR) Procedure. For a time-critical visit, this protocol applies where it differs from the Missed, Late and Short Visits Procedure.

rows: Time-sensitive medicine

A medicine that must be given or taken at a specific time because a delay or missed dose may lead to serious harm (the definition used in guidance based on NICE NG67), confirmed for that person by their prescriber or pharmacist.
Agreed time
The clock time of each dose, agreed with the person and the prescriber or pharmacist, and shown on the eMAR.
Window
The period around the agreed time within which the dose must be given: as set by the prescriber or pharmacist, or 30 minutes either side of the agreed time where they set none.
Time-sensitive medicine plan
The part of the medicines section of the care plan for one time-sensitive medicine, including the written advice on what to do if a dose is late or missed.
Time-critical visit
A visit at which a time-sensitive dose is due, or at which we give a meal or other support that a time-sensitive dose depends on.
Late or missed dose
Late: a time-sensitive dose given outside its window. Missed: not given at all, or not by the latest time the plan allows.

blocks.p: The Registered Manager, as medicines lead, is accountable for this protocol, declines in writing any dose time we cannot staff safely, and reviews every late or missed time-sensitive dose the day it is reported (the Deputy Manager in their absence). The Deputy Manager carries out the monthly time-critical visit audit.

subsections.heading: Care Coordinator and Field Care Supervisor

blocks.p: Authorised medicines assessors and eMAR users identify time-sensitive medicines, write each plan and set up the eMAR flag and window. The Care Coordinator plans, allocates and approves changes to time-critical visits, briefs care workers, and contacts prescribers and commissioners.

The member of Office staff named as monitor under the Lone Working and Staff Personal Safety Policy, and the On-call Manager out of hours, watch time-critical visits, act on late care workers, obtain clinical advice and record decisions.

subsections.heading: Care Workers and Senior Care Workers

blocks.p: They read the plan, arrive on time, give time-sensitive doses first and within the window, and phone the office as set out below.

The authorised medicines assessor identifies time-sensitive medicines at the medicines assessment under the Assessing Medicines Support Needs Procedure, whenever a medicine is started or changed, and at every hospital discharge. The assessor reads the label and leaflet, asks the person and family what happens when a dose is late, and checks each medicine against the list below. There is no national list, so the prescriber or pharmacist confirms which medicines are time-sensitive for this person and the window for each; the assessor records who confirmed it and when.

columns: Medicines the assessor always asks about
rows: Medicines for Parkinson's disease
Levodopa preparations such as co-careldopa and co-beneldopa, and other Parkinson's medicines taken at set times
Diabetes medicines linked to meals
Insulin, and diabetes tablets the label says to take with or just before food
Medicines for epilepsy
Anti-seizure medicines taken at fixed times
Steroid replacement
Hydrocortisone or prednisolone for adrenal insufficiency or long-term steroid dependence
Medicines that need a steady level at fixed intervals
Anti-rejection medicines after a transplant, HIV medicines, and antibiotics prescribed at set hours
Anything a health professional names
Any medicine the prescriber, pharmacist or a specialist nurse says must be given at a set time

bullets: Where the assessor is unsure, or the prescriber or pharmacist has not yet answered, the medicine is treated as time-sensitive with the default 30-minute window. The Care Coordinator asks the prescriber or pharmacist the same working day and records the answer in the care plan.
A medicine is taken off the time-sensitive list only on the prescriber's or pharmacist's written advice. Directions such as 'before food' do not on their own make a medicine time-sensitive.
Every time-sensitive medicine also carries the advice-if-declined flag under the Consent, Mental Capacity and Declined Medicines Policy.

blocks.p: Before we support the first dose, the assessor writes a plan for each time-sensitive medicine in the medicines section of the care plan, with the person and, where the person agrees or it is in their best interests, their family. It is approved with the care plan.

rows: What it is for
The condition, and what the medicine does for the person in their own words, for example 'helps me move and swallow'.
Dose and agreed times
Each dose and its clock time, fitted to the person's routine, meals and sleep, and any food instruction, for example 'insulin 15 minutes before breakfast, which we prepare'.
Window
The window, who set it and when.
Late or missed dose advice

The prescriber's or pharmacist's written advice: the latest time a late dose can still be given, whether a dose found missed is given or left out, and how the next dose is affected. Until it is received, every dose outside the window needs advice before it is given.
Warning signs

What a late or missed dose may look like for this person, such as stiffness, freezing, slurred speech or difficulty swallowing; shaking, sweating or confusion from low blood sugar; or a seizure, and which signs mean 999.
Who else is involved
Doses given by the person, family or a community nurse, how we learn they were given, and the specialist or community nurse to contact.
Contingency
Who to phone, whether a named adult relative who already gives this medicine could give a dose if we cannot reach the person in time, and what happens if there is no reply.

blocks.p: The person's missed-visit risk level is High under the Needs Assessment and Care Planning Policy. Their risk assessment in CareFlow records the harm a late or missed dose could cause and the contingency above.

An authorised eMAR user flags each time-sensitive medicine on the eMAR as time-critical, with the agreed times and the window set as the tolerance in minutes, second-checked before the first dose. Where a window differs either side, such as 'up to 15 minutes before a meal, never after', the tolerance is set to the shorter side and the full window written in the dose instructions. The Care Coordinator briefs care workers on a new or changed plan before their next visit to the person.
Visit times are fitted to dose times, not dose times to visits, unless the prescriber agrees to move a dose. The Care Coordinator applies these rules:

bullets: Marking: the visit is marked time-critical in CareFlow scheduling, which electronic call monitoring uses.
Planned start: 15 minutes before the agreed dose time, or at the opening of a window narrower than 15 minutes either side, so the 15-minute check-in trigger still leaves time to send someone else.

Allocation: only to a care worker with current medicines competency, signed off for every formulation due and, for a Level 3 task, for the person and task. Core care team members first; anyone else is phone-briefed by the Care Coordinator beforehand.

Travel: realistic travel time plus at least 10 minutes' spare. Never straight after a visit that depends on a second worker, or one that has overrun by 10 minutes or more at 3 or more visits in the last 2 weeks.
No clashes: a care worker is never given two time-critical visits whose windows cannot both be met.

Changes: only the Care Coordinator, or the On-call Manager out of hours, changes the time or care worker, after checking the window, competency and travel; care workers never swap, move or shorten these visits. A visit moves outside the window only with the prescriber's or pharmacist's agreement and the person's, recorded in the care plan.

Daily check: by 2pm each working day, within the daily cover check in the Missed, Late and Short Visits Procedure, the Care Coordinator checks that every time-critical visit to the end of the next working day has a care worker meeting these rules. Any still uncovered at 4pm goes to the Registered Manager or Deputy Manager. The On-call Manager checks at the start of each on-call period.
Shortages: time-critical visits come first, before other High missed-visit risk visits, and are never left uncovered to cover another visit (Business Continuity and Emergency Planning Policy).

blocks.p: Where our visits cannot meet the dose times, for example five Parkinson's doses a day, the Care Coordinator asks the prescriber or Parkinson's nurse the same working day whether the times can change, and asks the commissioner within 2 working days for the visits needed. The care plan records who gives each dose we do not.

When the person or family cancels a time-critical visit, the Care Coordinator (On-call Manager out of hours) confirms before the dose time who will give the dose and records it under the Visit Cancellations and Refusals of Care Procedure. If nobody will, the risk is explained and it is handled as a declined dose of a flagged medicine.

A care worker who may be late for a time-critical visit phones the office (On-call Manager out of hours) as soon as they know, once parked with the engine off. When a care worker says they will be late, or has not checked in 15 minutes after the planned start, Office staff or the On-call Manager act at once:

steps: Phone the care worker. If they can still give the dose within the window, confirm and record it.

Otherwise, send the nearest care worker who meets the allocation rules or, if none is free, a Field Care Supervisor, Senior Care Worker, Care Coordinator or the On-call Manager with current medicines competency.

Phone the person or named contact to say who is coming and when. Where the plan names an adult relative who already gives this medicine and they agree to give this dose, it is recorded as Family Administered with the time and who told us.

If the dose will be outside the window, tell the care worker going what the plan's late dose advice says; where it does not cover the situation, obtain advice from the prescriber or pharmacist, or NHS 111 out of hours, before the dose is given.
Record each call and decision on the visit's check-in/check-out record, and any dose advice in the daily visit notes.

blocks.p: Where the care worker has not been heard from, the worker-safety escalation in the Lone Working and Staff Personal Safety Policy runs alongside and never delays the dose.
Care workers follow the Administering and Supporting People with Medicines Procedure, with these steps for time-sensitive medicines.

steps: Check in on arrival, open the eMAR and, once the window is open, give time-sensitive doses before any other task.
Inside the window: give the dose and record it as Given straight away, so the actual time is recorded.
Before the window opens: do other tasks first and give the dose when it opens. If the visit would end first, phone the office before giving it.

Window closed, or closing before you can give it: phone the office before giving the dose, follow the advice and record it in the eMAR note. Never give a late dose, or a missed dose with the next one, on your own judgement. Wait for the call back up to 30 minutes after the planned end of the visit, while the office covers your next visit; if advice comes later, the office arranges an extra visit.

Declined, asleep where the care plan says not to wake them, unable to swallow, unwell, or the medicine is not in the home: record the matching outcome and phone the office before you leave, saying first that it is time-sensitive. The office obtains advice straight away and, for a missing medicine, a supply the same day.

Watch for the warning signs in the plan. Call 999 for the signs it names, a person who is hard to wake, or low blood sugar not improving after a second treatment (First Aid Procedure). Stay with the person and tell the office.
Double-handed visit: give the dose yourself if you are signed off for it; do not wait for the second worker.

No answer or no access: phone the office within 5 minutes of arriving, wait somewhere safe until it says you may leave, and follow the No Reply, No Access and Missing Person Procedure. The office tells everyone it contacts that a time-sensitive dose is due, and calls 999 if the person is not accounted for 15 minutes after your call.

sections.heading: When a dose is late or missed

bullets: Advice: every late or missed dose gets clinical advice straight away, from the plan's written advice or the prescriber or pharmacist (NHS 111 out of hours). Where NHS 111 advised, the Care Coordinator tells the GP practice by the end of the next working day.
People told: the person, and the named contact where the person agrees or it is in their best interests, are told what happened and the advice.
Next visit: the office briefs the next care worker on the advice, the next dose and the signs to watch for.

Incident: a late or missed dose is a medicines incident under the Medication Errors, Near Misses and Incidents Procedure, entered in the incident log by the care worker before the end of their shift where it happened at their visit; otherwise by Office staff the same working day, or the On-call Manager before the 10am handover. A dose taken late or not at all by the person's own choice follows the Consent, Mental Capacity and Declined Medicines Policy and is not in itself an incident.

Review and escalation: the Registered Manager or Deputy Manager reviews it the same day and grades it under the Incident Reporting, Investigation and Learning Policy, at least Medium where the dose reached the person late or not at all. Escalation to the Nominated Individual and Directors follows that policy and the Medicines Management Policy.

Patterns: two late or missed time-sensitive doses for one person within 4 weeks lead to a focused care plan and risk assessment review within 7 days, and the safeguarding lead considers whether it is neglect.

Supply: care workers tell the office the same day when a time-sensitive medicine has 7 days' supply or less and no new supply is in the home. The Care Coordinator confirms the next supply with the pharmacy, or the family where they order, within 1 working day (Ordering, Collecting, Storing and Disposing of Medicines Procedure).
Changes: when a time-sensitive medicine is started, stopped or changed, the plan and eMAR entry are updated and second-checked before the next dose and visit times re-checked.

Leaving hospital: before discharge, the Care Coordinator (On-call Manager out of hours) asks the ward when each time-sensitive medicine was last given and the next dose is due, and plans the first visit so the discharge medicines check under the Medicines Changes, Transfers of Care and Hospital Discharge Procedure is done and that dose given within its window.
Going into hospital: the care worker shows the eMAR to the ambulance crew, and the office tells the ward the same day which medicines are time-sensitive and their times.

blocks.p: Plans and professional advice are kept in the care plan, the contingency in the risk assessment, each dose with its actual time on the eMAR, office calls and decisions on the visit's check-in/check-out record, dose advice in the daily visit notes, and late and missed doses in the incident log, for the periods in the Records Management and Retention Policy.

blocks.p: The detail is in the Medicines Training and Competency Assessment Procedure. A care worker whose practice led to a late or missed dose reaching the person is reassessed under the Medicines Management Policy before further unsupervised medicines support.

blocks.p: Our targets are: 100% of time-sensitive medicines with an approved plan before the first dose; no missed time-sensitive doses; at least 98% of time-sensitive doses given within their window; and 100% of late or missed doses with clinical advice recorded. In a month below 98% the Registered Manager records the reason and an action in the service improvement plan and reports both to the next Monthly Quality and Governance Meeting.

This protocol is reviewed every 12 months by the Registered Manager and approved by the Directors under the Policy Management and Document Control Policy, and sooner after a change in law or guidance, a change to CareFlow time-critical flags, a serious incident, an inspection finding, or when monitoring shows it is not working.
